issues.legal_issue: Oral evidence cannot be used between parties to contradict or vary the sale consideration recorded in a written sale agreement.
material_facts: The written agreements recorded a sale consideration of Rs.45,000.
The seller alleged that the parties had actually agreed on Rs.3 lakhs and had recorded the lower amount to reduce stamp duty and registration charges.
The courts below rejected that allegation, and the Supreme Court found no reason to disturb their concurrent findings.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent findings rejecting the alleged oral agreement for a higher sale price were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Indian Evidence Act bars evidence of an oral agreement or statement between parties to a written contract when it is offered to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from the written terms. The Court applied that provision to uphold the concurrent findings.

predicates.appeal_from_concurrent_fact_findings: A party appealed after lower courts made concurrent findings on the facts.
predicates.written_contract_records_sale_price: The parties recorded the sale price in a written agreement.
predicates.party_offers_oral_term_to_change_sale_pr: A party relied on an alleged oral agreement to claim a sale price different from the one recorded in the written agreement.

issues.definition: When a party appeals concurrent findings after relying on an alleged oral term to change the sale price recorded in a written agreement, the finding rejecting that variation is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: Specific performance may be refused where the circumstances, including prolonged extensions, sharp property-value escalation, and hardship to the seller, make enforcement inequitable.
material_facts: The buyers paid most of the recorded sale consideration, but the agreements extended the time for performance repeatedly over a total period of eight years.
The second agreement recorded that the buyers had been unable to pay the balance and complete the sale within the earlier period.
The seller built a house on the property and lived there with his family; the property was his only property and shelter.
The property was in an urban area, and the Court considered the substantial increase in its value over the long passage of time.
The Court considered that enforcement would cause the seller and his family greater hardship than refusal would cause the buyers.
issues.conclusion: The decree for specific performance was set aside because granting that discretionary relief would be inequitable in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to aver and prove readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff's part of the contract at all material times. Under Section 20, specific performance is discretionary and is not granted merely because it is lawful to do so; the discretion must be exercised judicially in light of the circumstances, conduct of the parties, agreement recitals, and circumstances outside the contract. Relying on Sardar Singh v. Smt. Krishna Devi and Saradamani Kandaplan v. Rajalakshmi, the Court considered the totality of circumstances, including rapidly escalating urban property values and the hardship of enforcement after a long delay.

rule.if: suit_for_specific_performance and prolonged_extensions_of_performance and buyer_acknowledged_inability_to_complete and substantial_property_value_escalation and seller_occupies_only_home and enforcement_causes_greater_hardship_to_seller

predicates.suit_for_specific_performance: A buyer brought a suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.prolonged_extensions_of_performance: The parties repeatedly extended the time for completing the sale over a prolonged period.
predicates.buyer_acknowledged_inability_to_complete: The buyer's own conduct or recorded statement showed an inability to pay the balance or complete the sale within the agreed period.
predicates.substantial_property_value_escalation: The property substantially increased in value during the prolonged period before the dispute was decided.
predicates.seller_occupies_only_home: The seller and the seller's family live in a house on the property, which is their only home or property.
predicates.enforcement_causes_greater_hardship_to_s: Enforcing the sale would cause the seller greater hardship than refusing enforcement would cause the buyer.

issues.definition: When a buyer seeks specific performance after prolonged extensions and acknowledged inability to complete, and property-value escalation and the seller's housing circumstances make enforcement more harmful to the seller, specific performance is refused as inequitable.

issues.legal_issue: A buyer denied specific performance may nevertheless receive repayment of the advance and compensation in the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The buyers had paid an advance of Rs.42,500.
The Court refused specific performance but directed repayment of the advance with interest and payment of Rs.2,00,000 as compensation.
issues.conclusion: The seller was directed to repay the advance with interest and pay compensation to the buyers, even though specific performance was refused.
issues.legal_principle: The Court granted repayment and compensation as the appropriate relief on the facts after denying specific performance; it cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this monetary relief.

predicates.suit_for_specific_performance: A buyer brought a suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.buyer_paid_advance: The buyer paid money in advance under the sale agreement.
predicates.specific_performance_refused: The court declined to compel completion of the sale.

issues.definition: When a buyer seeking specific performance paid an advance and the court refuses to compel the sale, the advance is repaid with interest and compensation is awarded.
